sections.h2: Which office does what with your tax bill
sections.html:
Three county offices handle the same bill in turn. The Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets what a parcel is worth, the Sheriff's Office sends the bill and takes payment, and the County Clerk's Office keeps whatever goes unpaid.

Who handles a Henderson County property tax bill
OfficeJobWhen you deal with it
PVAValues the parcelAssessment questions and appeals
Sheriff's OfficeMails the bill, takes paymentFrom November 1 until the bill turns delinquent
County ClerkHolds uncollected bills, runs the tax saleAfter January 1 following the due date

Real estate notices are mailed in late October or early November, and the sheriff accepts payment from November 1. A bill turns delinquent on January 1 after its due date. The sheriff holds the file until uncollected bills are turned over to the clerk.

Delinquency depends on two things: the due date is behind you and any appeal rights have run out. If you are disputing a value, keep the appeal calendar and the payment calendar in front of you at the same time.

Henderson County sits in far western Kentucky on the Ohio River, across from Evansville, Indiana, and is part of the Evansville, IN-KY metro area. The city of Henderson is the county seat. The 2020 population was 44,793, and the latest estimate is 44,255.

The county has 20,295 housing units, and 64.9 percent of homes are lived in by their owners. About 37 percent of occupied homes were rented at the 2020 census, so there is a real rental market next to the owner-occupied majority. The middle owner home value is $171,900, and the middle gross rent is $777. Buyers who commute from here to Evansville often shop the whole metro area, which is worth remembering when you price.

sections.h2: Who to call for local questions
sections.html:
These local agencies come up most when a house is for sale.

  • The Henderson City-County Planning Commission oversees public and private development inside both city and county limits.
  • Henderson GIS offers maps, data and information on the county.
  • The Henderson Area Board of Realtors and the Housing Authority of Henderson are listed among community organizations.

If a buyer asks about zoning or development near your parcel, point them to the planning commission. Send questions about the tax bill itself to the sheriff or the PVA.

Interest and penalties begin, a lien attaches, and an outside buyer may purchase the debt. The steps run in this order.

  • The bill moves to the County Clerk's Office at 20 N Main Street, 2nd Floor, Henderson, where interest of 1 percent per month and penalties accumulate.
  • A lien stays on the property until payment in full.
  • Any individual or company qualified under KRS Chapter 134 may buy the bill at the clerk's tax sale. The clerk cannot predict or prevent that purchase.
  • The purchaser has 50 days to notify the owner. The owner then pays the purchaser, who sends a release to the clerk for recording.
  • A foreclosure suit by the purchaser becomes possible one year after the certificate of delinquency was created.

You can pay the clerk in person or mail a personal check, cashier's check, money order or certified check. Cards work for an added fee, and the clerk's number for details is 270-827-5753. American Express, Discover and MasterCard are taken, and Visa only as a debit.

Start with a conference at the PVA's office. KRS 133.120 puts that step ahead of any formal appeal. The conference happens during or before the inspection window, and the Department of Revenue may allow up to 25 extra days.

If the conference doesn't settle it, file a written petition with the county clerk. The appeals board holds a public hearing and fixes fair cash value, and the county attorney speaks for the state and county there. If you lose, you can go on to the Board of Tax Appeals, but only after appearing before the county board.

Anyone you pay to represent you must be an attorney, accountant, tax consultant, your own employee, a broker or a certified appraiser. They carry written authorization and disclose any contingency fee, although attorneys need not state its terms. The board can also raise a value, but it must first send you notice and a hearing date.

Whoever owns the property on January 1 gets the year's bill. Under KRS 134.015 the debt is personal to that owner, and a delinquency lien under KRS 134.420 outlasts any sale. Before the closing date, line up two numbers: what the sheriff shows for the current year and what the clerk shows for earlier ones.

If a prior year sits with the clerk, the 1 percent monthly interest becomes part of the payoff, so ask for a fresh figure close to the signing. The title agent can pay the total out of your proceeds. For recording charges and the real estate transfer tax on the deed, see the Henderson County Clerk page.

A cash sale skips the lender's payoff schedule, but it doesn't skip the lien. The tax still has to be cleared before the deed can pass free of it. If you are behind, getting the clerk's payoff letter early gives you time to decide whether to pay from savings or from the sale proceeds.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
Pull your last tax bill and any delinquency notice, and note whether the sheriff or the clerk currently holds the file. Bring photo ID if you plan to pay in person at 20 N Main Street. If you filed an appeal, keep the petition and hearing notice handy, since a buyer's lender may ask about an open dispute.

Ask the sheriff for the current-year amount and the clerk for any earlier years, and write both down with the date you called. Interest keeps running at 1 percent per month on anything held by the clerk, so a figure from early in the month may be stale by closing. If a lender is paying off a mortgage at the same table, tell the closer which years are still open so the tax lines are not missed on the settlement statement.

When the clerk's file is clean, the title search moves faster and closing is less likely to slip. When an outside buyer already holds the bill, expect the 50-day notice and the release step to add time, so start early. If you plan to appeal, ask the PVA's office how its conference is scheduled before you call anyone else, because that conference comes first and the petition to the county clerk follows only if it fails.

faqs.q: When does Henderson County start taking property tax payments?
faqs.a: November 1. Notices go out in late October or early November, and the sheriff accepts payment beginning that day. A bill goes delinquent on the following January 1.

faqs.q: Where is a delinquent Henderson County bill paid?
faqs.a: At the County Clerk's Office, 20 N Main Street, 2nd Floor Offices, Henderson, KY 42420. Mailed payments must be a check, money order or other certified funds.

faqs.q: How much interest does the clerk charge on a delinquent bill?
faqs.a: One percent per month plus penalties. A buyer of the bill at the tax sale may add charges allowed under Kentucky law.

faqs.q: Can someone else buy my delinquent Henderson County tax bill?
faqs.a: Yes. Any person or company qualified under KRS Chapter 134 can buy it at the clerk's sale, and the clerk can neither predict nor stop the purchase.

faqs.q: How long before a bill buyer can foreclose?
faqs.a: One year after the certificate of delinquency is created. Some buyers wait longer while the property's equity covers the debt.
